question: What evidence is there about how clients under 40 choose a financial advisor?

claims.text: UBS's next-generation study (published 2026-04-22) reports that experience and expertise top the next generation's wish list when choosing a wealth manager (79%). More than half (56%) want advisors who can build trusted relationships across generations, and 41% want an advisor who fully understands the next generation's needs. The study also reports a gender split: women emphasize experience (90%), frequent engagement (35%) and early commitment to the next generation (40%), while men more often prioritize a deep understanding of their financial goals (49%).

UBS (published 2026-04-22) also reports that two-thirds (67%) of the next generation say a strong personal connection with their advisor is important. Women place greater weight on personal fit and regular contact, while men focus on competitive pricing and specialist expertise.

Cerulli (published 2025-10-29) says younger investors are typically more comfortable directing their own investing through online brokerages. It concludes that advisors trying to reach these prospects must be able to articulate benefits outside investing, such as financial planning, lending and tax services.

Fidelity's 2025 Investor Insights Study (published 2025-10-09) covers wealthy Gen X, Y and Z households. It says they value advisors but seek transparency in advisor compensation, broader life guidance beyond investment management, and emerging investment products such as active ETFs, liquid alternatives and cryptocurrencies. It describes them as focused on holistic financial planning and life goal achievement.

Schwab's Q3 2025 call (published 2025-10-16) says Gen Z investors are turning to Schwab partly because Schwab is meeting them in the channels where they turn for information about investing. Management said it knows they learn about finances primarily through social media and family, and that their top online resource is YouTube. Management calls Schwab the number one financial services firm on YouTube by followers. This is management's own account of why younger clients choose Schwab.

The GSAM alternatives survey (published 2025-10-17) reports that financial media is the most common information source for individual investors, followed by advisors, and that Millennials cite social media more often while Boomers rely on traditional outlets. This is about information sources on alternatives, not advisor search.

The CFPB-cited misinformation survey (published 2025-06-06) found that Americans aged 25-45 are more trusting than those aged 46-64 of financial information from generative AI tools (44% vs. 26%) and social media (44% vs. 24%). Overall, people are most confident in information from a qualified advisor such as a CFP® professional.

UBS (published 2026-04-22) reports that younger adults (22 to 25 years) rely most on peers (57%) as a source of advice in succession planning. On the family's banker, 41% prefer to work with their family's existing bank.

Cerulli (published 2025-10-29) finds just 41% of HNW practices say their clients' children are either established clients or actively involved in the planning process. HNW executives say advisors' relationships with clients' children have been slipping slightly since 2020.

Morgan Stanley's CFO said on the 2Q26 call (published 2026-07-15) that for clients who do not yet have an advice-based relationship, the firm is working on a referral model. She said it can begin as early as financial education and with 401(k) assets coming in through workplace. This is a firm statement of approach, not evidence on how younger clients choose.

The Edward Jones 2025 10-K (published 2026-03-13) lists, among its initiatives, a new digital platform focused on attracting and retaining Next Generation investors. It says the Partnership cannot reliably predict the timing or outcome of its initiatives.

Bank of America's Private Bank 2026 Study of Wealthy Americans (published 2026-06-17) covers Gen Z and Millennials aged 21 to 45. It reports that 67% believe traditional stocks and bonds can no longer deliver above-average returns, and 88% say they are likely to allocate more to alternatives in the next few years (vs. 15% of Boomers and Silents). It also reports that 32% of Gen Z and Millennials have a prenuptial agreement, vs. 15% of Gen X and 4% of Boomers and Silents, and says planning is starting earlier among younger married investors.
UBS (published 2026-04-22) reports that most next-generation respondents (83%) favor a blended approach to communicating, combining digital convenience with in-person interaction.

Schwab's Q3 2025 call (published 2025-10-16) says one-third of retail households that created a financial plan within the last two years are under the age of 40. Management says the average age of its clients continues to get younger.

The Edward Jones 2025 10-K (published 2026-03-13) names, as a risk, changing client expectations for expanded product offerings and technology needs, and changing client demographics, preferences and values. It also names competition from firms offering enhanced digital experiences and lower-cost computer-based "robo-advice", and says clients can transfer their business to competitors at any time.

UBS's next-generation study (published 2026-04-22) reports that when succession planning involves private banking partners, 41% prefer to work with their family's existing bank, 31% want a new provider and 29% are open to switching. UBS's respondents are next-generation members of wealthy families.

Edward Jones's 10-Qs for the second quarter (published 2025-08-08) and third quarter (published 2025-11-07) of 2025 attribute elevated asset outflows partly to an aging client base and generational wealth transfers outside the firm. The Q2 filing says the net new asset decrease was attributable to existing clients.
Morgan Stanley's CEO said on the 4Q24 call (published 2025-01-16) that the firm retains 99% of its clients. This is not split by age or by inheritance.

Schwab's CEO said on the 3Q26 call (published 2026-10-15) that its retention rate around wealth transfers is extremely high. The accompanying deck (published 2026-10-15) shows about 75% of assets retained in a wealth transfer event. These are management's own figures.

Cerulli (published 2025-10-29) says notable differences in service preferences among women and next-generation clients are likely to shift market share to the firms best prepared to meet their needs. It warns advisors of the risks that wealth transfers pose to their practices.

adjacent.text: Wealthtender's advisor-search survey (published 2025-08-13) found that 97% plan to interview multiple advisors and 96% will do further research online before hiring. It found 83% research the advisor's reputation through online reviews and awards, and 64% want to know the advisor's areas of specialization and 62% the fee/pricing structure before making contact. Among sources people use to find advisors, the survey lists AI search tools (25.40%), social media (22.20%), online advisor directories (31.80%), financial institutions (49.00%) and referrals from professionals (49.20%).
adjacent.differs_because: The survey covers American consumers generally and the chunks shown do not break results out for clients under 40, so it describes advisor selection broadly, not younger clients specifically.

adjacent.text: Schwab management said on the 3Q26 call (October 2026) that approximately 70% of new-to-firm retail households are Gen Z and millennials. On the 4Q25 call (January 2026) it said nearly 60% of Gen Z-led new accounts opened in 2025 are under 40. The 2Q25 call (July 2025) said nearly 60% of new-to-firm clients are under 40.
adjacent.differs_because: These figures show how many younger households joined Schwab, mostly as self-directed retail investors. They do not show the criteria younger clients use to select an advisor.

adjacent.text: Vanguard research (published 2025-06-04) reports that 86% of advised clients had more peace of mind than when managing their own finances. It reports 88% among clients with a human advisor and 69% reporting significant increases among digital-advice clients.
adjacent.differs_because: It covers all advised clients, not those under 40, and measures emotional value rather than what younger clients expect when choosing an advisor.

gaps.what: No age-split data (under 40 vs. older) on the factors mass-market or affluent retail clients use to select an advisor. The closest evidence covers wealthy next-generation heirs (UBS, Fidelity) and general consumers (Wealthtender).
gaps.suggested_source: Cerulli, JD Power, Fidelity or Vanguard investor surveys cut by age; firm-commissioned client research

gaps.what: No under-40 breakdown of how clients find advisors (referral, parent's advisor, online search, social media). The Wealthtender channel data is not split by age.
gaps.suggested_source: Wealthtender study methodology and cross-tabs by age; firm new-client source data

gaps.what: No direct evidence on fee preferences or hybrid-advice preferences of clients under 40 in the mass-affluent segment. Only the UBS blended-communication result and the Fidelity compensation-transparency theme are available, both for wealthy next-generation households.
gaps.suggested_source: Cerulli or Vanguard studies of Millennial/Gen Z advice preferences; the full Fidelity 2025 Investor Insights white paper

gaps.what: No firm discloses the rate at which heirs under 40 keep or leave an inherited advisor. Retention figures are not split by age of heir, and the reasons for leaving come only from the UBS survey and firm risk statements.
gaps.suggested_source: Cerulli wealth-transfer retention research; firm disclosure on assets retained after transfer by heir age
